deep_searches.goal: Identify published studies that model or measure the relationship between water depth, buoyancy-reduced wheel normal force, hydrodynamic resistance, and maximum available tire traction for a vehicle moving through water. Determine whether any study closes, or provides the components needed to close, the loop from increasing water depth and flow to reduced normal force and available tire force during motion.
deep_searches.name: Dynamic Vehicle Traction in Floodwater
deep_searches.summary:
The literature contains the force balance needed to relate flooding to loss of mobility, hydrostatic buoyancy reduces the tire-supported normal load while drag/lift and rolling resistance set the opposing demand, but only a few moving-vehicle studies couple these terms dynamically; full-scale traction measurements make [Smi19, Smi17] the strongest experimental anchor, and coupled CFD-multibody models provide the clearest computational closure [Yam24b, Was15].

TWO COMPLEMENTARY REGIMES.
- Flood/ford stability: available longitudinal/lateral resistance is typically represented as tire-surface friction times BUOYANCY-REDUCED NORMAL LOAD, compared with flow-induced drag (and, where material, lift). Full-scale tests directly measured traction under varying buoyancy and surface conditions (concrete, gravel, sand) and measured/modelled drag [Smi19]; scaled moving-car experiments resolve buoyancy, drag, frictional and rolling resistance, identifying transitions to sliding or flotation [Sha20, Sha19d, Sha21].
- Tire-scale flooded pavement: hydrodynamic pressure can additionally unload or separate the tire from pavement. Experiments and FSI models quantify the effects of water depth, normal load, speed and slip on longitudinal/cornering force and hydroplaning [Din10, Mal19, Sri13, Naz20]. THIS SUPPLIES A DEPTH- AND SPEED-DEPENDENT TIRE-FORCE LAW RATHER THAN A FIXED FRICTION COEFFICIENT.

CLOSURE AND REMAINING GAP. CFD-MBD/SPH frameworks resolve fluid loads, suspension/wheel contact and motion jointly [Was15, Paz16, Yam24b]; [He26d] adds free-running shallow-water and flume-load validation. These are the most direct route to a closed depth/flow to wheel-load to tire-force to motion loop. Most flood-hazard studies instead close a quasi-static incipient-sliding/flotation balance [Kell92, Shu11, Xia11b, Arr15], or prescribe/limit vehicle motion. Off-road egress models explicitly include buoyancy, suspension, soil reaction and wheel loading [Slo69, Jur74].

deep_searches.name: Quantitative Flood Traversability Connections
deep_searches.summary:
A PHYSICS-RESOLVED TRAVERSABILITY PIPELINE IS MOST VALUABLE AS A CALIBRATED, PROBABILISTIC LINK-PERFORMANCE MODEL, NOT A NEW BINARY CLOSURE RULE, whose outputs can propagate from vehicle state to network accessibility, climate-conditioned reliability, and automated-driving operating limits [Con18, He24, Lee20b].

PRIORITIZED CONNECTIONS.
1. Road-network functionality and partial failure. Map simulated speed, immobilization/stability margin, and time-to-recover onto link severity/capacity rather than closure; then evaluate isochrones, critical-facility access, and topology/flow consequences [He24, Gan22, Zha19]. VIDEO-DERIVED DEPTH-SPEED FUNCTIONS PROVIDE AN IMMEDIATELY USABLE EXTERNAL BENCHMARK [Pre17], while transport-model validation exists at city scale [Du24].
2. Reliability and fragility surfaces for vehicle operations. TREAT MPM PARAMETER SWEEPS AND RECONSTRUCTION UNCERTAINTY AS DISTRIBUTIONS OVER LIMIT STATES (loss of traction, flotation, displacement, stalled vehicle), YIELDING P[LS | h, v, slope, vehicle, t] RATHER THAN DETERMINISTIC DEPTH-VELOCITY BANDS [Con18, Lam18]. Existing full-scale and laboratory stability evidence anchors thresholds [Smi19, Mil20], but uneven beds, flow angle, leakage, and transient flood fronts remain major transfer gaps; unsteady forcing can raise drag 40-50% [Azh26].
3. Climate-conditioned scenario and stress-test layer [Wan24, Pre17b, Nas00]; satellite-video extent/velocity validation offers an independent hydraulic check [Mas24].
4. ADS operational-design-domain and policy layer. Encode flood state, uncertainty, vehicle class, and acceptable residual risk as an executable, graded ODD membership with speed restriction, rerouting, minimal-risk maneuver, or exclusion, not merely "safe/unsafe" [Sch21, Sal22, Cha24].

deep_searches.goal:
I have a weakly-compressible particle-method (material point method) simulation of a rigid sphere held at a fixed depth in water, and I am grading it against a high-precision published floating-sphere heave-decay benchmark. The measured vertical fluid force on the sphere exceeds the analytic buoyancy by roughly 35 to 64 percent, consistently, across six runs and four averaging windows. The implementation has been verified: the force and the analytic denominator both recompute from raw particle geometry to machine precision, so this is not an arithmetic or bookkeeping error.

I need to determine what physically or numerically causes a particle-method buoyancy force to be overestimated by tens of percent, and specifically how to distinguish between three competing explanations that I cannot currently separate.

FIRST EXPLANATION, which I most need help testing: the error may not be in the force at all, but in the DENOMINATOR, because the analytic buoyancy is computed from a measured free-surface elevation and my surface estimator deliberately excludes all particles within two sphere radii of the body axis. That annulus is exactly where the surface is depressed or elevated by the body's presence and where the pressure generating the vertical force acts. A surface-elevation offset of under two centimetres, which is about one grid cell, would account for the entire discrepancy with no error in the solver at all.

SECOND EXPLANATION: genuine over-prediction of hydrostatic or hydrodynamic force by weakly compressible particle methods.

THIRD EXPLANATION: the boundary or coupling treatment at the rigid body, including whether zeroing grid momentum at a wall distorts stress into the body over several cells, and whether the reported force is contaminated by the contact or restitution treatment rather than being a clean pressure integral.

For each explanation I want diagnostic tests that would DISTINGUISH it from the others, ideally cheap ones runnable on an existing dataset.
deep_searches.name: free surface elevation estimator error in particle method buoyancy validation
deep_searches.summary:
The literature supports treating the 35-64% excess as three separable error channels, surface reconstruction, pressure/hydrostatics, and body-boundary coupling, rather than as evidence of a single "MPM buoyancy error"; the canonical target remains the high-precision floating-sphere benchmark [Kra21b].

SURFACE ESTIMATOR AND DENOMINATOR. Near-body exclusion is not established as a benign operation: particle methods identify free surfaces through density/neighbor criteria, geometric scans, or reconstructed signed-distance/level-set fields [Mar10b, Liu22f, Sun19g, Zha17c], and the literature emphasizes false surface classification and truncated support as pressure-error sources [Got09b, Che18c]. A cheap discriminator is to recompute elevation with nested exclusion radii (including zero), local vertical columns, and a geometric/level-set reconstruction; compare the resulting analytic buoyancy directly with the same raw force. A BODY-OFF HYDROSTATIC RUN PROVIDES THE ESTIMATOR BIAS INDEPENDENTLY OF BODY LOADING.

PRESSURE AND COUPLING. WCMPM exhibits volumetric locking and interface pressure oscillation [Che18c], while MPM spatial integration and particle-location errors can distort stresses [Ste00, Bau23]. For a fixed sphere, decompose the load into pressure, viscous, contact/penalty, and restitution contributions, and compare the pressure profile with p = p0 + rho*g*z. Repeat under resolution, sound-speed, and boundary-method changes. Traditional MPM wall momentum zeroing can distort stress several grid lengths into an object; image-particle boundaries reduce this artifact [Sch19e]. SPH work likewise attributes force/pressure errors to boundary deficiency and pressure extrapolation [Gar19, Ban18, Jou20]. The retrieved studies mostly report improved validation, not a documented 35-64% buoyancy failure traced uniquely to one cause; controlled ablations are therefore essential.

deep_searches.name: GPU particle solver portability scaling and surrogate fidelity
deep_searches.summary:
Published evidence supports 10-50 million-particle runs with multi-GPU SPH and MPM, but does not establish current ARM64 build/run status for the mainstream codes or provide apples-to-apples A100/H100 versus Grace Hopper results; the clearest Grace Hopper result is the SWIFT SPH prototype at 15 million particle-updates/s with near-perfect strong scaling across four nodes [Nas25b].

SOLVER AND SCALING LANDSCAPE.
- DualSPHysics is open-source CUDA/C++ SPH with multi-GPU MPI support; published demonstrations reach 32 million particles, although on legacy hardware [Cre15, Val12]. GPUSPH likewise supports multi-GPU clusters, while recent work reports CUDA/Clang compiler trade-offs rather than ARM validation [Bil18, Bil22b].
- Portable MPM options are better represented by Kokkos-based Karamelo and the performance-portable MPI/OpenMP/CUDA framework of Qiu et al.; neither paper proves a complete Grace Hopper deployment [Buc24, Qiu22]. Multi-GPU MPM studies report 100 million particles on four GPUs and 134 million on eight, plus 1.01 billion particles across eight workstations, but not on A100/H100 [Wan20d, Qiu22]. A separate MPM implementation reports ~1280x speedup on 16 GPUs [Don18].
- THE SUPPLIED LITERATURE NEITHER CONFIRMS THAT THE CITED SPH PACKAGE IS INTRINSICALLY X86-ONLY TODAY NOR DOCUMENTS AN ARM-HOST CUDA BUILD FAILURE; code-specific rootless containers are also not reported. Generic ARM rootless-container overhead is low, but this is not solver evidence [Med24b].

SURROGATES AND VALIDATION GAPS. MPM-trained GNS studies report 5% trajectory error and 5000x speedup, or 700x with subspace reduction, but use granular/obstacle problems, not a fluid-rigid-body incipient-motion verdict [Kum22, Hae21]. NO CITED WORK PRESERVES A DISCRETE THRESHOLD, AND NO CITED STUDY REPORTS THE SAME VEHICLE/FLOW CASE INDEPENDENTLY IN MPM AND SPH WITH FORCE-COEFFICIENT DISAGREEMENT; existing vehicle studies compare one solver against experiments or other CFD [Azh23, Alq23].

deep_searches.goal: I run GPU material point method simulations of a passenger vehicle in floodwater, and every run so far has held the vehicle stationary in a flow while I vary depth and velocity. For each such study I want to know whether the vehicle motion was kinematically prescribed or solved from the hydrodynamic load, and if solved, what rigid body integrator was used and how the force and torque were extracted from the fluid solver. I want to know how wheel contact was represented, because my vehicle is a watertight hull discretised as rigid particles with no wheels, no suspension and no rolling degree of freedom, and full scale experiments report roughly an order of magnitude difference between locked wheel friction near 0.3 and free rolling resistance near 0.024. I also need practical numbers: particle counts, grid sizes, wall clock time per second of simulated physics, GPU hardware, and whether the work was single or multi GPU. Studies that report a moving vehicle simulation failing to match experiment are especially useful.
deep_searches.name: moving vehicle floodwater GPU particle simulation
deep_searches.summary:
Published moving-vehicle work separates into prescribed-trajectory wading studies and genuinely coupled fluid-rigid-body dynamics: the former dominate automotive CFD, while the latter are concentrated in MBD-SPH frameworks that solve vehicle motion, contact, and friction [Was15, Paz16, Maz18, Can18].

- PRESCRIBED MOTION: SPH/CFD wading studies vary entry speed, depth, or wheel rotation but generally report loads and water ingress rather than a vehicle whose speed is solved dynamically [Zha21i, Xin21b, Var22]. The most relevant flood-stability simulation reports a full-scale passenger vehicle moving across incoming flow, with floating instability at 0.38 m depth and a depth-velocity threshold of 0.39 m2/s, BUT THE AVAILABLE RECORD DOES NOT EXPOSE ITS MOTION ALGORITHM OR WHEEL MODEL [Alq22]. Experimental non-stationary benchmarks cover 1:10 vehicles at 0.047-0.089 m depth and 0.20-0.39 m/s [Sha19d]. No clear published speed-depth map for a self-propelled vehicle entering water emerges here.
- SOLVED MOTION: [Was15] resolves suspension, wheels, steering, axles, drivetrain, tire/ground and tire/fluid contact with penalty and asperity friction; [Paz16] applies distributed point-cloud FSI forces; [Maz18] uses half-implicit symplectic integration and a cone-constrained optimization solve; [Can18] couples DualSPHysics to Project Chrono's nonsmooth DVI solver.
- REPRODUCIBILITY GAP: the supplied studies do not report, in one place, particle/grid counts, GPU model, wall time per simulated second, multi-GPU scaling, or a runnable x86/CUDA vehicle case. [Can18] is explicitly open-source; [Hu18] supplies two-way rigid coupling for MLS-MPM but is not a vehicle-wading study.

deep_searches.goal: I am building a numerical simulation of a passenger vehicle MOVING through a flooded roadway, in order to produce something the field appears to lack: a graded "safe crossing speed" surface as a joint function of water depth, floodwater flow velocity, and the vehicle's own travel speed. The existing vehicle-stability literature is almost entirely threshold-based and is derived from a STATIONARY vehicle exposed to flow. I need to know what has actually been done when the vehicle itself moves. I especially want papers that describe how the hydrodynamic force on the moving body is extracted and validated, and whether they operate in the body-fixed (moving reference frame) or ground-fixed frame. I also want anything on moving-reference-frame formulations for particle methods such as the material point method, and on refinement windows that follow a moving body through a large domain. My understanding is that this may be genuinely unaddressed, and I want to know whether that is true.
deep_searches.name: moving vehicle floodwater simulation open source implementations
deep_searches.summary:
The literature contains only a small, distinct moving-vehicle evidence base: Shah's 1:10 Perodua Viva experiments varied vehicle motion and flow Froude number, reporting speed-dependent drag, buoyancy, friction and an incipient-velocity criterion [Sha18c, Sha19d, Sha20, Sha21], while Al-Qadami et al. added full-scale coupled CFD of a passenger car crossing incoming flow [Alq21, Alq22]. These studies still reduce stability to failure thresholds, not a continuous safe-speed surface resolving vehicle speed independently from current velocity; other vehicle-wading CFD generally prescribes speed and emphasizes water ingress or resistance [Ols18b, Xin21b, Var21].

REUSABLE IMPLEMENTATIONS.
- Open-source SPH/MBD coupling is the strongest directly reusable route: DualSPHysics [Cre15] with Project Chrono/DVI coupling [Can18, Maz18] and Chrono::FSI vehicle-fording models [Paz14, Paz16, Was15].
- OpenFOAM-based moving-body options include dynamic/overset meshes [Jas10, She15], FloatStepper with released code and added-mass treatment [Roe23], and signed-distance immersed boundaries (sdfibm) [Zha20o]. IBAMR provides open-source immersed-boundary/Brinkman multiphase implementations with force constraints rather than surface-stress integration [Bha19]; AMR moving-body IB is explicitly demonstrated in [Nan19].
- BODY-FIXED FORMULATIONS ARE ESTABLISHED FOR EULERIAN IB/LEVEL-SET SOLVERS [Yan09, Yan10] BUT ARE NOT EVIDENT AS A DEVELOPED MOVING-REFERENCE FORMULATION FOR MPM. MPM free-surface, rigid-coupling, and AMR components exist [Zha17c, Li22b, Hu18, Mao16], BUT A BODY-FOLLOWING REFINEMENT WINDOW APPEARS UNREPORTED.

VALIDATION ASSETS. Public or reproducible targets include full-scale/model vehicle tests [Alq21, Sha20], dam-break cylinder data with pressure/video supplements [Kam19], and a high-precision public floating-sphere decay dataset [Kra21b].

deep_searches.goal:
I am validating a material point method (MPM) fluid solver against static buoyancy, and it fails badly in a way I do not understand. A rigid sphere of radius 0.15 m is held FIXED at its design waterline, so it is exactly half submerged, in a tank of weakly compressible water. I measure the vertical reaction force on the sphere from the momentum exchange between the fluid and a signed-distance-function (SDF) collider: the solver accumulates the impulse needed to project fluid velocities out of the solid region, and divides that accumulated impulse by the timestep to report a force.

The measured vertical force is about 50 percent LARGER than the analytic buoyancy rho*g*V_submerged. I have ruled out two explanations. First, particle leakage: fluid particles were penetrating the tank floor, and after two independent boundary fixes that reduced leakage from 4.5 percent of all particles to 0.008 percent (49 particles out of 598505), the force overestimate is still about 36 percent. So eliminating 99.8 percent of the leak removed only 30 percent of the force error. Second, domain confinement: quadrupling the tank plan area changed the measured ratio by only 1 percent, so it is not a wall or bounded-domain artifact.

Relevant numerics: the equation of state is weakly compressible of the form pressure = -K*(J^-gamma - 1) with an artificially reduced sound speed of about 13 m/s rather than the physical 1500 m/s, so the peak Mach number is well below 1 but the fluid is far more compressible than real water. The basis is a quadratic B-spline. The sphere spans roughly 16 grid cells across its diameter. Gravity is 9.81 m/s^2.

I want to understand what systematically causes a large positive bias in the measured steady vertical force on a fixed submerged or floating rigid body in material point method and in smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations. Candidate causes I want assessed against the literature include: the artificially reduced sound speed and the choice of equation of state and its effect on the hydrostatic pressure field; the method used to extract the coupling force, specifically momentum or impulse exchange through a velocity projection compared with integrating the pressure field over the wetted surface, and whether the impulse-exchange route systematically double counts gravity or inertial terms for a body held fixed; particles-per-cell, spatial resolution and the number of particles resolving the flow depth; the treatment of the free surface and the zero-pressure boundary condition there; and quadrature error or the cell-crossing and null-space errors associated with the basis functions.

I also want to know how published papers actually validate hydrostatic buoyancy and floating-body equilibrium in particle and hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian methods. Specifically: what canonical benchmark problems are used for static buoyancy and for floating-body heave decay, what quantitative error against the analytic or experimental value those papers report and treat as acceptable, how they measure the force on the body, how long they run and over what window they average, and what convergence study they present. My aim is to replicate an established published validation case exactly, with its own reported tolerance, rather than continuing to invent my own benchmark and my own pass criteria.
deep_searches.name: MPM SPH buoyancy force overestimation and hydrostatic validation benchmarks
deep_searches.summary:
The strongest literature signal is that a large positive buoyancy bias is more plausibly a discrete hydrostatic/interface-coupling error than a tank-size effect, but the supplied studies do not establish a universal 50% bias or show that velocity-projection impulse exchange intrinsically double-counts gravity [Yan17, Yan18, Ste00, Bau23]. In MPM, hydrostatic validation is explicitly used to expose integration, pressure-oscillation, volumetric-locking, and cell-crossing errors; quadratic B-splines and generalized interpolation reduce these errors but do not eliminate particle-location and quadrature sensitivity [Ste00, Ste08, Wal07, Che18c]. Reduced-sound-speed WCMPM is a credible contributor through compressibility and pressure transients, while incompressible/projection MPM was introduced specifically because WCMPM performs poorly at free surfaces; the retrieved papers provide no quantitative mapping from sound speed to steady buoyancy bias [Zha17c]. Free-surface pressure treatment is similarly central: level-set pressure conditions and continuous rather than discontinuous free-surface treatment improve hydrostatic/pressure behavior [Zha17c, Ski13]. SPH work confirms that boundary treatment, pressure formulation, resolution, and domain geometry materially affect body loads [Gar19, Jou20, Gun14].

The most reproducible published floating-body benchmark is Kramer et al.'s 300-mm sphere, ballasted to half submergence, with three heave-decay amplitudes and public time-series data; experimental uncertainty is about 0.3% of drop height, but this is a MOTION benchmark, not a stated static-force tolerance [Kra21b, Sci19]. For static verification, MPM hydrostatic columns/problems and SPH still-water pressure or fixed/floating-cylinder tests are more direct [Yan17, Gar19, Omi17, Qui18b]. The retrieved literature rarely reports force-extraction windows, pressure-surface versus impulse-exchange cross-checks, or systematic particles-per-cell convergence, leaving those as essential diagnostics for the present case.

deep_searches.name: Multi-resolution MPM for Large-domain Flooding
deep_searches.summary:
The literature contains credible local-resolution MPM for solids and free-surface fluids, but NO DEMONSTRATED MPM STUDY WAS FOUND THAT FOLLOWS A RIGID VEHICLE WITH A REFINEMENT WINDOW THROUGH A LARGE FLOOD DOMAIN; the closest fluid result is dynamic AMR for free-surface waves and breaking WITHOUT a vehicle [Mao16], while adaptive MPM-FSI work is preliminary and not road-scale flooding [Hu10].

CLOSEST STRUCTURAL MATCH: dynamic AMR [Mao16] and moving mesh management [Shi10] reduce active cells but DO NOT establish near-floor accuracy, particles-per-cell control, or moving-body refinement. GIMP/SAMRAI nested grids [Ma05], structured GIMP refinement [Ma06], mesh grading [Lia15], hierarchical B-spline MPM [Zha21g] and local BSMPM bridging [Sun20d] are PREDOMINANTLY SOLID-ONLY. [Zha21g] uses splitting, WHICH IS UNSAFE FOR HISTORY VARIABLES unless deformation-gradient transfer is defined.
MOST TRANSFERABLE COST REDUCTIONS: sparse active grids [Qiu22, Zha26s] and dynamic meshing [Shi10] cut memory and work when the domain is empty, BUT DO NOT REDUCE THE SMALLEST-CELL EXPLICIT TIMESTEP OR RESOLVE THE FLOOR LAYER. Hybrid 3-D MPM / 2-D shallow-water coupling [Pan23c] and MPM-finite-volume depth-averaging [Zhe23d] address FAR-FIELD cost, not vehicle-scale near-floor physics.
[Ste08] IS DECISIVE: fixed particles-per-cell can LOSE convergence under grid refinement. Methods must co-refine or control PPC, otherwise AMR silently changes quadrature and transfer conditioning. Standard MPM, GIMP, CPDI and B-spline MPM CANNOT BE TREATED INTERCHANGEABLY; nonuniform grids already produce projection error [Wal07], and boundary stability can impose harsher CFL limits [Bai22, Ni20].
ADJACENT: adaptive SPH supplies the strongest moving-body precedent, splitting, merging, shifting and geometry-following refinement [Mut21, Hu18, Haft22], but its remedies require reformulation for MPM's deformation gradient and history-dependent stress. NO MOVING-REFERENCE-FRAME MPM RESULT WAS IDENTIFIED; open-boundary MPM exists [Zha19e].

deep_searches.summary:
Photo-derived vehicle meshes can already support rigid-body collision simulation when their exterior envelope is tessellated adequately, but the literature contains little vehicle-specific end-to-end work linking reconstruction, collision-proxy repair, and validated inertial properties; [Ros15] is the direct simulation precedent, while [Eri13] establishes photo-based vehicle mesh accuracy.

GEOMETRY-TO-COLLIDER PIPELINE.
- Acquire metrically anchored exterior geometry. SfM/photo scanning produces an explicit vehicle mesh [Eri13]; neural reconstruction can improve mesh-detail fidelity relative to tested photogrammetry and LiDAR workflows [Far25b]. For deformed bodies, laser point-cloud surface reconstruction uses undeformed regions and vehicle dimensional references, REPORTING MEAN SIGNED DEVIATIONS OF +1.36 AND -1.14 CM against the original body [Che14].
- Extract or repair a physics representation rather than use rendering geometry directly. Surface-aligned Gaussian splatting supports rapid Poisson mesh extraction and optional joint mesh-appearance refinement [Gue23]. Non-manifold inputs can be converted to volumetric collision proxies without watertight preprocessing [Su26]; collision-aware convex decomposition preserves interior and boundary collision conditions [Wei22].
- TREAT APPEARANCE GEOMETRY, CONTACT GEOMETRY, AND INERTIAL PARAMETERS AS DISTINCT ASSETS. General Real2Sim pipelines jointly infer mesh/collision geometry and inertial parameters from visual reconstruction plus interaction [Pfa25], whereas Gaussian-mesh joint optimization can refine geometry and physical parameters from trajectories [Mor25].

VEHICLE DYNAMICS CALIBRATION AND VALIDATION. Vehicle mass, CG, and full inertia must be measured or independently estimated: INERTIA ERRORS MATERIALLY AFFECT 3-D COLLISION TRAJECTORIES [Mac97]. Measured EV datasets and empirical estimators provide current reference values [Pre24]; InTenso+ supplies pendulum-based mass-property measurement and CAUTIONS THAT SIMPLE ESTIMATORS ARE INADEQUATE FOR ACCURATE DYNAMICS [Gob14]. The most relevant validation hierarchy is: dimensions/surface deviation against trusted vehicle geometry [Eri13, Che14], collider convergence through tessellation and contact-response comparison to established vehicle models [Ros15], then trajectory/displacement sensitivity to independently cross-checked mass properties [Mac97, Pre24].

deep_searches.name: Physics Simulation Validation Protocol
deep_searches.summary:
DECISION CREDIBILITY, NOT NUMERICAL AGREEMENT, IS THE GOVERNING ENDPOINT: A FORD CLAIM REQUIRES VALIDATED SIX-DOF OUTCOMES AND A CONSERVATIVE MARGIN TO THE HAZARD THRESHOLD, WHEREAS A NO-FORD CLAIM MAY BE ISSUED WHENEVER UNCERTAINTY SPANS OR EXCEEDS THAT BOUNDARY [Obe04, Eca20, Eas01].

EVIDENCE CHAIN.
- Component verification. Test 3DGS reconstruction against surveyed/known road geometry where available; test MPM separately on analytical flow, dam-break/free-surface, contact, and rigid/elastic-obstacle cases. Report conservation residuals, contact penetration, interface position, pressure/force histories, and convergence, not merely visual plausibility. MPM particle/grid crossing, locking, and stress/pressure oscillation require explicit checks [Bra11, Vau20, Aco19, Coo18]; published dam-break and FSI datasets can substitute for new experiments [Aur23, Sun19c, Zha17].
- Calibration versus validation. Freeze parameters after calibration on a disjoint reference subset; compare held-out trajectories, yaw/roll/pitch, wheel contact/loss, hydrodynamic loads, and threshold-relevant maxima against vehicle-water experiments where available [He26d]. AT EACH VALIDATION POINT REPORT SIGNED DISCREPANCY AND A VALIDATION INTERVAL COMBINING REFERENCE-DATA, NUMERICAL, AND PARAMETER UNCERTAINTY; THIS ESTIMATES MODEL ERROR RATHER THAN PRODUCING A BINARY "VALIDATED" STATUS [Eca20, Col97].
- Numerical and parametric uncertainty. For representative corners and decision-boundary cases, perform at least 3 grid/particle and timestep refinements; report observed order, Richardson/GCI intervals, and iterative residual criteria for every decision quantity [Roa94, Cel07, Ste01]. Propagate depth, velocity, friction/contact, water properties, reconstructed geometry, and model-form alternatives; RETAIN ALEATORY VERSUS EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY SEPARATELY [Mul16, Whi19].
- Held-out stress and decision testing. Reserve strata from the sweep, especially threshold-adjacent and extreme cases, BEFORE tuning. Treat the sweep as ODD coverage, not exhaustive proof [Neu20, Wei23, Gyl20]. Issue FORD only when a conservative bound remains within all civil thresholds across the declared ODD; otherwise label NO-FORD or indeterminate, with operational limits and evidence traceability in a UL/SOTIF-style safety argument [Koo23, Put23].

deep_searches.goal: My simulation of a vehicle in floodwater produces a binary engineering verdict: whether the vehicle begins to move or stays put. I have limited supercomputer time and I want to spend it on physical realism that actually changes that verdict rather than on realism that only improves how the result looks. I need the literature ranked by measured effect on an incipient motion or flotation threshold, with the effect size and its source, and I need to be told plainly where nobody has measured it. The specific effects I care about are these. First, road surface geometry: camber, crown, gutter, kerb and longitudinal grade, and whether anyone has demonstrated that a crowned or cambered road changes a vehicle stability threshold compared with a flat plane. My computational cell is about 0.15 metres and real road surface texture depth is a few millimetres, roughly one fiftieth of a cell. Second, free surface fidelity: air entrainment, spray formation, surface tension and turbulence closure. Third, water compressibility: I use a reduced bulk modulus giving a numerical sound speed around 13 metres per second, which is below the common guideline that it should exceed ten times the maximum flow velocity. Fourth, outlet boundary conditions for free surface particle methods. Fifth, vehicle watertightness and underbody detail.
deep_searches.name: which realism effects change a flood vehicle stability verdict
deep_searches.summary:
Road/tyre friction and vehicle watertightness have the clearest demonstrated power to change a flood-stability verdict; slope and flow orientation also matter, whereas NO RETRIEVED STUDY QUANTIFIES A CROWNED OR CAMBERED ROAD AGAINST A FLAT PLANE [Smi19, Kra16, Azh23, Mil20, Boc19].

EFFECTS WITH THRESHOLD EVIDENCE.
- Bed condition/friction: full-scale tests measured traction on concrete, gravel, and sand and found materially different friction coefficients, requiring a worst-case value; SPH rough-bed studies validate velocity and shear-stress fields, but do not report a vehicle motion-threshold shift or a resolved-versus-effective-roughness error [Smi19, Kaz16, Kaz20, Shi19].
- Road slope/orientation: a conceptual model includes terrain slope, and experiments show stability depends on flow angle; a 5% grade study reports buoyancy onset at 0.055 m model depth, not a flat-road comparison [Mil20, Kra16, Sha19d].
- Watertightness: watertight models produce higher floating depths at prototype scale, while reviewed stability thresholds vary substantially with watertightness; no retrieved source isolates a sealed-versus-flooding threshold difference in metres [Kra16, Boc19].
- Unsteady free surface: simulated drag rises 40-50% under accelerating flow, but this is not a discrete verdict comparison [Azh26].

EFFECTS WITHOUT A DEMONSTRATED VERDICT SHIFT. No retrieved study shows air entrainment, spray, surface tension, turbulence closure, reduced sound speed, or outlet-boundary choice flipping vehicle motion. Compressibility papers document wave/impact sensitivity, not a move/no-move flip; THE TEN-TIMES-FLOW-SPEED RULE HAS NO PRIMARY DERIVATION HERE [Dal07, Vic12, Sdi00]. SPH outlet studies provide characteristic, buffer, pressure, and traction formulations, but do not establish a minimum sufficient condition for steady discharge or vehicle stability [Las09, Vac12, Neg19, Taf18, Hol20].

deep_searches.summary:

- REPRODUCIBLE STATE: declarative environments, containers, dependency manifests and provenance graphs. deep_searches.name: Settling and Force Reporting in Free Surface Flow
deep_searches.summary:
NO UNIVERSAL FRAME COUNT OR FORCE-SETTLING THRESHOLD EMERGES: the defensible protocol is to detect and exclude initial and final transients, demonstrate stationarity for the reported observable, and attach uncertainty based on correlated samples [Bro19, Ber21d, Lon05].

[1] DECAY TO STATIONARITY. Fixed-body and disturbed-free-surface studies support OBSERVABLE-SPECIFIC gates, energy/damping decay, stable mean and bandwidth, or automated truncation, NOT universal times [Sch85, He24d, Puj24, Cho15, Oli24]. Autocorrelation, integrated correlation time, blocking and bootstrap convert a stationary record into an effective sample size [Fly89, Gro18, Jon18, Dur20]. Tank practice waits for measured residual-wave levels, with the first sloshing mode governing inter-run offset time [Jen21, Tho07].

[2] FINITE-DURATION MOVING PASSAGES. For ship resistance, report a PRESPECIFIED constant-speed interior window, its mean, filter and window sensitivity, and correlated uncertainty [Cal80, Doc08, Ste15, Bro19]. This is a protocol, not a transferable run length. SLAMMING, WATER ENTRY AND IMPACT LOADING GENERALLY HAVE NO STEADY FORCE: report peak distributions, impulses, envelopes or event statistics with repeat-run uncertainty. Evidence for a universally accepted moving-body settling criterion remains thin.

[3] THRESHOLD DECISIONS. Incipient motion is PROBABILISTIC AND RECORD-LENGTH DEPENDENT; define a movement probability or activity rate with detection uncertainty, not a single critical stress [Lav87, Nei69, Dan02, Dip10].

NUMERICAL REPRODUCIBILITY. Non-associative, order-dependent reductions can produce small drift OR ALTER DISCRETE GATES; fixed-order or sorted reproducible reductions and higher-precision accumulation mitigate this [Xu19b, Ahr15, Sik24]. Repeated runs should report outcome spread and gate-pass frequency; NO UNIVERSAL REPEAT COUNT EXISTS, and independent-start ensembles are the stronger convergence check [Sto18b, Wie11, Zha23].

deep_searches.goal: I am an undergraduate researcher producing a computational fluid dynamics style simulation result that will be defended in a paper and a poster, and I want to know how professional computational scientists actually audit work like mine before publishing it. My records are short, roughly ninety to three hundred output frames, and when I apply established equilibration and stationarity tests the effective sample size comes out between three and forty. I have found that a quantity I reported to five significant figures moved and changed sign when I simply reran at a longer record length, and that a ratio I was comparing against a published benchmark spans more than a factor of three across plausible choices of bed friction and grid resolution, with the flow regime itself changing as I refine the grid so that a grid convergence study is confounded. I want to know what the established practice is for reporting a discrete or classification outcome from a simulation whose underlying continuous quantities are not converged. I want to know how researchers handle the situation where the only available validation benchmark is at a completely different physical scale, three orders of magnitude apart in my case. Finally I want to know how negative and null results from simulation studies are reported credibly, because several of my own findings are refutations of my own earlier claims.
deep_searches.name: how computational researchers audit and defend simulation credibility
deep_searches.summary:
Credibility is a context-of-use claim built from separate evidence about code correctness, numerical solution accuracy, physical-model adequacy, and uncertainty, NOT a binary property conferred by agreement with one benchmark [Obe02b, Roy11, Mor19c].

DECISION-RELEVANT UNCERTAINTY.
- Richardson/GCI estimates are defensible only in an asymptotic refinement regime; NONMONOTONE OR NONCONVERGED RESULTS SHOULD BE TREATED AS NUMERICAL UNCERTAINTY, NOT REDUCED TO SPURIOUS SIGNIFICANT FIGURES [Roy10, Phi14, Log05].
- For a binary vehicle-movement verdict, THE USEFUL OBJECT IS THEREFORE A ROBUSTNESS OR FAILURE-PROBABILITY STATEMENT OVER RECORD LENGTH, FRICTION, RESOLUTION, AND MODEL ASSUMPTIONS. Threshold-based validation explicitly relates comparison error to DISTANCE FROM THE ENGINEERING THRESHOLD [Har17]. Correlated finite records must also carry sampling uncertainty [Oli12].
- A scale-mismatched benchmark supports only PARTIAL validation unless a hierarchy of simpler, shared-physics tests links it to the target; extrapolation uncertainty is a central unresolved problem [Oli14, Hil13, Rie20].

PARTICLE-METHOD EVIDENCE. No universal particle-method minimum has been adopted [Bra11]. A credible SPH case normally combines manufactured-solution/order tests, boundary-condition verification, conservation/stability checks, refinement studies, and validation of the coupled free-surface/solid physics [Neg21e, Neg22, Vac20]. Vehicle studies illustrate the value and limits of combining SPH with experiments [Azh23]; published stability thresholds themselves vary substantially across models and conditions [Boc19].

AUDITABILITY AND FAILURE MODES. Reproducibility requires versioned code, inputs, parameters, environment, hardware/parallel settings, workflow, and output provenance [Lei20b, Kra21, Dhr23]; CROSS-ARCHITECTURE AGREEMENT IS EVIDENCE OF ROBUSTNESS, NOT PHYSICAL VALIDITY, because rounding and parallel ordering can alter trajectories [Sen08, Gop21]. DOCUMENTED TRAPS INCLUDE AGREEMENT FOR THE WRONG REASONS [Ber18b] and underestimated iterative error [Eca20b]. NULL OR SELF-REFUTING RESULTS ARE STRONGEST WHEN REPORTED AS SENSITIVITY, UNCERTAINTY, AND DECISION-BOUNDARY FINDINGS RATHER THAN BURIED, consistent with validation being non-binary [Eas01].

deep_searches.name: Small Data Physics Surrogates at 36 Conditions
deep_searches.summary:
For 36 independent depth-velocity-vehicle conditions and scalar displacement/FORD outcomes, THE DEFENSIBLE BASELINE IS A LOW-DIMENSIONAL GAUSSIAN-PROCESS/KRIGING RESPONSE SURFACE (with a separate GP classifier or state-selecting model for FORD), NOT a trajectory-level GNS or neural operator; its uncertainty is directly relevant to interpolation and ITS EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZE IS THE 36 CONDITIONS, NOT THE 90 FRAMES OR MESH/PARTICLE COUNT [Cur91, Mec01, Con07, Bon21].

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS AT N=36.
- Deterministic computer-experiment emulation is explicitly designed for sparse input-output runs; kriging has remained robust across designs and sample sizes, whereas parametric ROM work finds DNN accuracy data-hungry and kriging comparatively strong [Sim01b, Ni23].
- THERE IS NO TRANSFERABLE NUMERICAL "MINIMUM N": adequacy depends on fill distance, response smoothness/nonstationarity, output discontinuities, and the required error near the FORD boundary [Haa14, Loe09, Pic10].
- POD/ROM and neural operators solve a different problem when trained to reconstruct fields or trajectories; their many spatial/temporal snapshots do not create independent macro-conditions [Swi19, Nay25].

VALIDATION AND SCOPE OF CLAIMS.
- Random condition splits are poorly aligned with structured interpolation and CAN LEAK NEARBY GRID NEIGHBORS. Fit/tune with leave-one-condition-out (LOCO); use standardized LOOCV residuals and predictive-interval calibration [Wee25, Con07, Kle19].
- Add leave-one-depth-row-out (and analogously velocity-column-out) as the more stringent sensitivity analysis: omit only interior rows for an interpolation claim; omitting either boundary tests extrapolation and should be reported separately.
- Pooling the three known vehicle classes with mass/dimensions as inputs is defensible for interpolation within those classes. IT CANNOT SUBSTANTIATE TRANSFER TO AN UNSEEN VEHICLE CLASS, only three class levels exist.
- Treat GP variance as a diagnostic, not proof: calibrate against blocked residuals, flag high uncertainty/near-threshold cases [Via10, Fuh20, Bic08].

deep_searches.summary:
A defensible FORD / NO-FORD result REQUIRES CLASS-SPECIFIC GEOMETRY and experimentally anchored force-stability validation, NOT a common Yaris hull with relabelled mass: buoyancy, drag and lift lever arms, wheel normal loads and sliding/float/roll thresholds depend jointly on displaced volume, underbody shape, wheelbase, track and centre of mass [Smi19, Mar17, Arr15, Alq22].

CLASS-SPECIFIC STATE REQUIRED: distinct geometry for hull dimensions and the submerged-volume curve, wheel locations, track and wheelbase, wetted and projected areas, contact patches, CoM and inertia, hence buoyancy, drag and lift moments, axle loads, traction and rollover margins. MASS ALONE MAY BE SCALED ONLY AFTER geometry-specific hydrostatics and inertia are established; regressions supply provisional CoM/inertia estimates, NOT VALIDATION [All03]. CLAIM-GRADE VALIDATION: verify force/momentum, hydrostatic equilibrium, free-surface dam-break/slosh and rigid-contact convergence BEFORE vehicle cases [Sun19c, Li14, Roa94]. Report experimental, parameter and discretisation uncertainty SEPARATELY [Obe04, Roy11, Cel07].

NO RETRIEVED RECORD reports calibration or subtraction of a smeared wall layer, an accepted correction protocol, or a defensible minimum number of cells across shallow water. No single threshold, and no evidence for GIMP/CPDI eliminating this error, can be inferred.

10.1002/aic.15868.abstract: The two-fluid model (TFM) has become a tool for the design and troubleshooting of industrial fluidized bed reactors. To use TFM for scale up with confidence, the uncertainty in its predictions must be quantified. Here, we study two sources of uncertainty: discretization and time-averaging. First, we show that successive grid refinement may not yield grid-independent transient quantities, including cross-section–averaged quantities. Successive grid refinement would yield grid-independent time-averaged quantities on sufficiently fine grids. Then a Richardson extrapolation can be used to estimate the discretization error, and the grid convergence index gives an estimate of the uncertainty. Richardson extrapolation may not work for industrial-scale simulations that use coarse grids. We present an alternative method for coarse grids and assess its ability to estimate the discretization error. Second, we assess two methods (autocorrelation and binning) and find that the autocorrelation method is more reliable for estimating the uncertainty introduced by time-averaging TFM data. © 2017 American Institute of Chemical Engineers AIChE J, 63: 5343–5360, 2017
10.1002/aic.15868.authors: M. Syamlal, I. Celik, and S. Benyahia
10.1002/aic.15868.title: Quantifying the uncertainty introduced by discretization and time-averaging in two-fluid model predictions

10.1002/cav.70024.abstract: The expression of fine details such as fluid flowing through narrow pipes or split by thin plates poses a significant challenge in simulations involving complex boundary conditions. As a hybrid method, the material point method (MPM), which is widely used for simulating various materials, combines the advantages of Lagrangian particles and Eulerian grids. To achieve accurate simulations of fluid flow through narrow pipes, high‐resolution uniform grid cells are necessary, but this often leads to inefficient simulation performance. In this article, we present an adaptive boundary material point method that facilitates adaptive subdivision within regions of interest and conducts collision detection across grids of varying sizes. Within this framework, particles interact through grids of differing resolutions. To tackle the challenge of unevenly distributed subdivided particles, we propose a surface reconstruction approach grounded in the color distance field (CDF), which accurately defines the relationship between the particles and the reconstructed surface. Furthermore, we incorporate a mesh refinement technique to enrich the detail of the mesh utilized to mark the grids during subdivision. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in simulating various materials and boundary conditions, and contrast it with existing methods, underscoring its distinctive advantages.
10.1002/cav.70024.title: An Adaptive Boundary Material Point Method With Surface Particle Reconstruction

10.1002/fld.5233.abstract: With a view to simulating the entire process of a landslide‐triggered tsunami, ranging from tsunami generation to offshore wave propagation, with relatively low computational costs, we present a 2D–3D coupling strategy to bridge 3D MPM–FEM hybrid and 2D shallow water (SW) simulations. Specifically, considering the difference in basis functions between the 3D and 2D analysis methods, we devise a novel variable passing scheme in the domain overlapping method, in which a slightly overlapped domain enables the generated wave to pass through the connection boundaries with as little discrepancy as possible. For the tsunami generation stage in the 3D domain, the hybrid method combining the finite element method (FEM) and material point method (MPM) is adopted. In this method, the 3D governing equation of the solid phase is solved with the MPM, whereas the well‐established 3D stabilized FEM is applied to that of the fluid phase in an Eulerian frame. Additionally, the phase‐field method is employed to track the free surface of the 3D fluid domain. On the other hand, the SW equation that represents the offshore wave motion in the 2D domain is solved by the 2D stabilized FEM. Several numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed scheme in properly passing the data from 3D/2D to 2D/3D domains.
10.1002/fld.5233.journal: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Fluids
10.1002/fld.5233.title: Variable passing method for combining 3D MPM–FEM hybrid and 2D shallow water simulations of landslide‐induced tsunamis

10.1002/nag.3731.abstract: The material point method (MPM) is often applied to large deformation problems that involve sharp gradients in the solution field. Representative examples in geomechanics are interactions between soils and various “structures” such as foundations, penetrometers, and machines, where the displacement fields exhibit sharp gradients around the soil‐structure interfaces. Such sharp gradients should be captured properly in the MPM discretization to ensure that the numerical solution is sufficiently accurate. In the MPM literature, several types of locally refined discretizations have been developed and used for this purpose. However, these local refinement schemes are not only quite complicated but also restricted to certain types of basis functions or update schemes. In this work, we propose a new MPM formulation, called the mapped MPM, that can efficiently capture sharp gradients with a uniform background grid compatible with every standard MPM basis function and scheme. The mapped MPM is built on the method of auxiliary mapping that reparameterizes the given problem in a different domain whereby sharp gradients become much smoother. Because the reparameterized problem is free of undesirably sharp gradients, it can be well solved with the standard MPM ingredients including a uniform background grid. We verify and demonstrate the mapped MPM through several numerical examples, with particular attention to soil‐structure interaction problems.
10.1002/nag.3731.authors: Yidong Zhao, Minchen Li, Chenfanfu Jiang, and J. Choo
10.1002/nag.3731.journal: International Journal for Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics
10.1002/nag.3731.title: Mapped material point method for large deformation problems with sharp gradients and its application to soil‐structure interactions

10.1002/nag.70048.abstract: The computational cost of the material point method (MPM) primarily arises from the information transfer between material points and the grid. In some high‐precision simulations, using a globally high‐resolution background grid and sufficient material particles per cell (PPC) can severely reduce computational efficiency. Many problems in geomechanics focus on local large deformations or failures, making global refinement an unsuitable choice. To address these issues, this study introduces a novel multi‐resolution material point method (MR‐MPM). This approach constructs MPM models at different resolution levels using bounded material points that connect these levels. By enforcing positional deviations of bounded material points through the penalty function, the high‐resolution and low‐resolution models are linked together, achieving local refinement. During implementation, it is only necessary to map the penalty forces of bounded material points to the corresponding level background grids. No other modifications are required, and no local equations need to be solved. Furthermore, this study derives a penalty factor value that eliminates the influence of material elastic modulus and background grid spacing, effectively simplifying parameter adjustment. Finally, a series of classical numerical examples, including elastic and elasto‐plastic cases, are used to verify the algorithm’s accuracy, convergence, and efficiency. The results predicted by MR‐MPM closely match finite element reference solutions and demonstrate good convergence. Compared to globally refined MPM, MR‐MPM significantly improves computational efficiency. These features give MR‐MPM great potential in large‐scale simulation analyses involving large local deformation, such as tunnel excavation, submarine landslides, and similar events.

10.1002/nme.6312.abstract: A local grid refinement scheme for the material point method with B‐spline basis functions (BSMPM) is developed based on the concept of bridging domain approach. The fine grid is defined in the local large‐deformation regions to accurately capture the complex material responses, whereas other spatial domains are discritized by coarse grids. In the overlapping domain between the fine and coarse grids, the constraint of particle displacements obtained with different grids is enforced using the Lagrange multiplier method to eliminate the spurious stress reflection at the fine/coarse grid interface. Representative numerical examples have shown that the BSMPM simulations with the proposed local grid refinement scheme could provide the solutions in good agreement with those obtained with the uniformly fine grid, and that no significant spurious stress reflection is induced at the fine/coarse grid interface, even for the bridging domain size as small as the cell size of the fine grid. It is also found that the proposed local grid refinement method can significantly reduce the BSMPM computational time compared with the cases for uniformly fine grids. A multitime‐step algorithm is presented and shown to considerably enhance the efficiency of the present local grid refinement scheme with no compromise in accuracy.

10.1002/nme.6312.journal: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
10.1002/nme.6312.title: A local grid refinement scheme for B‐spline material point method

10.1002/nme.6506.abstract: The material point method (MPM) combines Eulerian method and Lagrangian method and thus both Lagrangian particle position and interaction between neighboring Eulerian grid cells will affect the simulation stability. However, the original critical time step formula in the standard MPM does not reflect the effect of particle position and neighboring cell interaction on stability and overestimates the critical time step so much that the CFL number has to be very small, even smaller than 0.1, to obtain a stable solution at extreme particle positions. Therefore, in many engineering applications, the standard MPM is very expensive due to the small CFL number. In this article, the effect of particle position and neighboring cell interaction on stability of the explicit MPM is studied. An explicit critical time step formula is obtained based on the system eigenvalues in one dimension, and is then extended to two and three dimensions. For extreme deformation problems, the geometric stiffness matrix is taken into consideration which modifies the sound speed of particles in the critical time step formula. Several tests are performed to verify our formula and show a decrease in amount of time steps used for simulation with our formula comparing with the original formula.

10.1002/nme.6506.title: A precise critical time step formula for the explicit material point method

10.1002/nme.70210.abstract: The study of debris‐fluid‐structure interaction (DFSI) poses challenges for engineers and animators alike due to its complex nature involving multiple materials, multiple phases, constitutive nonlinearity, and large deformations across varying scales. Current numerical methods frequently overlook critical aspects of DFSI, can be overly complicated to implement, and require excessive computational resources for practical applications. To alleviate this problem, this paper introduces a flexible and explicit Material Point Method (MPM) that achieves a 100‐fold improvement over traditional MPM formulations in terms of CPU‐based computation. The key improvement results from the implementation of computer graphics techniques (MLS‐MPM, APIC, ASFLIP, Simple F‐Bar) and hardware (Multiple Graphics Processing Units). However, while computer graphics prioritizes qualitative realism, engineering needs quantitative accuracy. Therefore, this paper concentrates on a series of DFSI validation benchmarks using an enhanced graphics tool for engineering applications. Carefully chosen examples highlight critical aspects of DFSI. To show stability and favorability for next‐generation scales, we simulate 100,000 to 1,000,000,000 particles within hours for all benchmarks. Accuracy relative to experiments, analytical equations, and alternative numerical models is demonstrated.

10.1002/nme.70210.journal: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
10.1002/nme.70210.title: Validating High‐Performance Multi‐GPU MPM for Debris‐Fluid‐Structure Interaction

10.1002/nme.7217.abstract: The material point method (MPM) is a robust numerical simulation approach for continuum mechanics problems involving large material deformations coupled to changing surface topographies. These types of problems are present in many different engineering contexts, from understanding the failure processes of earthen slopes to predicting the strengths and failure mechanisms of body armor to modeling the impact forces of waves in fluid tanks. By using a set of persistent material point tracers to follow the motion and deformation of the continuum material while solving the equations of motion on a static simulation grid, the MPM avoids several shortcomings of more traditional numerical approaches including blurring of material surfaces — as in Eulerian finite element or finite volume methods (FEMs or FVMs) — and mesh tangling — as in Lagrangian FEMs. Despite its robustness, MPM is known to develop significant numerical errors: namely, (i) the particle ringing instability and (ii) solution dependent discretization and integration errors. In this work, we present an analysis of local‐in‐time, spatial integration errors in the MPM and several techniques designed to mitigate these errors. Error mitigation approaches previously described in the literature are compared to a new method we propose for problems involving very large material deformations. The proposed method is shown to offer substantial improvement over standard MPM for simulations of fluid‐like materials without requiring significant augmentation of existing MPM frameworks.
10.1002/nme.7217.authors: Aaron S. Baumgarten and Ken Kamrin
10.1002/nme.7217.journal: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
10.1002/nme.7217.title: Analysis and mitigation of spatial integration errors for the material point method

10.1002/nme.7347.abstract: The material point method (MPM) is frequently used to simulate large deformations of nearly incompressible materials such as water, rubber, and undrained porous media. However, MPM solutions to nearly incompressible materials are susceptible to volumetric locking, that is, overly stiff behavior with erroneous strain and stress fields. While several approaches have been devised to mitigate volumetric locking in the MPM, they require significant modifications of the existing MPM machinery, often tailored to certain basis functions or material types. In this work, we propose a locking‐mitigation approach featuring an unprecedented combination of simplicity, efficacy, and generality for a family of explicit MPM formulations. The approach combines the assumed deformation gradient ( F¯ ``` math \overline{\boldsymbol{F}} ``` ) method with a volume‐averaging operation built on the standard particle–grid transfer scheme in the MPM. Upon explicit time integration, this combination yields a new and simple algorithm for updating the deformation gradient, preserving all other MPM procedures. The proposed approach is thus easy to implement, low‐cost, and compatible with the existing machinery in the MPM. Through various types of nearly incompressible problems in solid and fluid mechanics, we verify that the proposed approach efficiently circumvents volumetric locking in the explicit MPM, regardless of the basis functions and material types.
10.1002/nme.7347.authors: Yidong Zhao, Chenfanfu Jiang, and J. Choo
10.1002/nme.7347.journal: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
10.1002/nme.7347.title: Circumventing volumetric locking in explicit material point methods: A simple, efficient, and general approach

10.1002/stvr.1912.abstract: Practical problems in scientific computation that solve differential equations rarely have explicit exact solutions. Therefore, verifying the correctness of such programs has long been a challenge due to the difficulty of producing expected outputs on test cases. In this paper, the principles of metamorphic testing are applied to verify programs that solve second‐order elliptic differential equations. We present a testing process specifically tailored for the verification testing of scientific computation programs and integrate it to the process of developing scientific software. Unlike existing approaches, we formally derive metamorphic relations from the numerical models of differential equations built in development process of scientific computing programs. The experimental results clearly show that our approach is effective in detecting faults commonly found in scientific computing programs. It outperforms the fault detecting ability of the trend method, which is a traditional testing method for scientific software.
10.1002/stvr.1912.title: Metamorphic Testing on Scientific Programs for Solving Second‐Order Elliptic Differential Equations

10.1006/jcph.2002.7103.abstract: The material point method (MPM) for solid mechanics conserves mass and momentum by construction, but energy conservation is not explicitly enforced. Material constitutive response and internal energy are carried on discrete points (material points), while the governing equations are solved on an overlying grid. The constitutive response (and internal energy) may be updated at the beginning or end of a numerical time step without affecting mass or momentum conservation properties. Both versions of the algorithm have been applied in the literature. Here energy conservation on the material points is investigated and found to depend strongly on the version of the algorithm used. The energy error is found and partitioned into two terms, one of which is of definite sign (and dissipative). The other term is indefinite, and of opposite sign for the two algorithmic variations. It is shown analytically for a single-material-point free-vibration example that one version of the algorithm is strictly dissipative. For the other version the error terms cancel each other out and energy is conserved. The same trends are borne out in numerical solutions of free axial vibration of continuum bars as the wavelength of the vibrational mode begins to approach the computational cell size. The dissipative algorithm may be described as tending to damp out unresolved modes. For resolved modes, both algorithms give identical results, with no perceptible energy error or dissipation. It is suggested that the dissipative algorithm is a better choice in general, as the damping is consistent with the accuracy of the solution.
10.1006/jcph.2002.7103.title: Energy Conservation Error in the Material Point Method for Solid Mechanics

10.1007/s00348-021-03151-5.abstract: Challenges for steady and unsteady model motion in a large water towing tank and procedures to overcome them are the focus of the presented work. Some challenges are attributed to experiments conducted in water, whereas others are uniquely ascribed to a towing tank facility. Data convergence and outlier detection are studied based on the phase averaged pressure in order to ensure proper data quality. Pressure measurements are performed with non-surface mounted sensors. Therefore, inertia effects are detrimental when the attached tubing is not fully de-aired. A procedure for de-airing the pressure sensor cavity and its tubing is described. An iterative approach is developed that compensates for nonlinear distortion of the model’s velocity profile. Further, vibration effects are examined by distinguishing mechanical and flow-induced frequencies that scale with the instantaneous model velocity. Sloshing waves are excited, which are a function of the water basin size. The first sloshing mode defines the required sensor offset time in between test cases when prevailing sloshing waves have not fully decayed. This appropriate selection of sensor offset time reduces data scatter and enables a reasonable waiting time in between test cases. A skim plate installed just below the water surface offers a potential solution to alleviate surface wave effects over the model.

10.1007/s00466-019-01783-3.abstract: Stress inaccuracies (oscillations) are one of the main problems in the material point method (MPM), especially when advanced constitutive models are used. The origins of such oscillations are a combination of poor force and stiffness integration, stress recovery inaccuracies, and cell crossing problems. These are caused mainly by the use of shape function gradients and the use of material points for integration in MPM. The most common techniques developed to reduce stress oscillations consider adapting the shape function gradients so that they are continuous at the nodes. These techniques improve MPM, but problems remain, particularly in two and three dimensional cases. In this paper, the stress inaccuracies are investigated in detail, with particular reference to an implicit time integration scheme. Three modifications to MPM are implemented, and together these are able to remove almost all of the observed oscillations.

10.1007/s10664-026-10840-4.abstract: Unit testing is essential for software reliability, yet manual test creation is time-consuming and often neglected. Although search-based software testing improves efficiency, it produces tests with poor readability and maintainability. Although LLMs show promise for test generation, existing research lacks comprehensive evaluation across execution-driven assessment, reasoning-based prompting, and real-world testing scenarios. This study presents the first large-scale empirical evaluation of LLM-generated unit tests at the full class level, systematically analyzing four state-of-the-art models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, and Mixtral 8x7B) against EvoSuite across 216,300 generated test cases targeting Defects4J, SF110, and CMD (a dataset mitigating LLM training data leakage). We evaluate five prompting techniques–Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL), Few-Shot Learning (FSL), Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), and Guided Tree-of-Thought (GToT)–assessing syntactic correctness, compilability, hallucination-driven failures, readability, code coverage metrics, and test smells. Reasoning-based prompting particularly GToT significantly enhances test reliability, compilability, and structural adherence in general-purpose LLMs. However, hallucination-driven failures remain a persistent challenge, manifesting as non-existent symbol references, incorrect API calls, and fabricated dependencies, resulting in high compilation failure rates (up to 86%). Moreover, test smell analysis reveals that while LLM-generated tests are generally more readable than those produced by traditional tools, they still suffer from recurring design issues such as Magic Number Tests and Assertion Roulette, which hinder maintainability. Overall, our findings indicate that LLMs can serve as effective assistive tools for generating readable and maintainable test suites, but hybrid approaches that combine LLM-based generation with automated validation and search-based refinement are required to achieve reliable and production-ready test generation.
10.1007/s10664-026-10840-4.title: Prompt engineering in LLMs for automated unit test generation: A large-scale study

10.1007/s12665-025-12501-z.abstract: Reproducibility across diverse high-performance computing (HPC) environments remains a major challenge in computational science, particularly for complex, multi-physics simulation workflows. This study presents a comprehensive approach to achieving bit-for-bit result reproducibility in the context of the OpenGeoSys (OGS) simulation suite. Given the widespread use of OGS in environmental science applications such as safety assessments for radioactive waste disposal and the optimisation of geothermal energy systems our approach enhances the reliability, transparency, and acceptance of simulation results in these safety-critical domains, shown in a case study for far-field deep geological repository assessment. We use GNU Guix to define fully declarative, verifiable software environments and deploy them as portable Apptainer containers, enabling consistent execution across multiple HPC systems. Leveraging AiiDA for workflow automation and provenance tracking, we conduct simulations and complex simulation workflows on three heterogeneous clusters, confirming identical binary-level outputs. The results demonstrate that reproducible and portable software environments can offer a pathway toward long-term verifiability in scientific high-performance computing. We also show how full data provenance originating from software source code and model input data resulting in full simulation workflow result data can be achieved.

10.1016/bs.aams.2019.11.001.abstract: Abstract It has been 25 years since Sulsky and her coworkers developed the first version of the material point method (MPM): a quasi particle method to solve continuum mechanics problems. In the MPM, the continua are discretized by Lagrangian particles moving over a fixed Eulerian background grid. As a result, large deformation and contact can be treated effortlessly. Since then, many improved instances of the MPM have been developed and the MPM has found applications in many fields from geoengineering to movie industry. As the MPM has now been matured and a large body of literature on it exists, it is a good time to ponder and reflect on the developments of the method to date. To this end, this manuscript provides a concise introduction to the MPM, covering theory, implementation, and applications. All the algorithms required to have a working MPM implementation for the simulations of solids, fluids, and their interactions are provided. We have coded these algorithms in in-house open source programs and used them to study the performance of different MPM variants for large deformation solid mechanics problems. These problems exhibit large plastic deformation, fractures and contacts. Convergence of different MPMs (CPDI, GIMP, B-splines, total Lagrangian MPM, improved MPMs) are studied. Furthermore, MPM formulations for fluids/gases and heat conduction are also covered. Potential areas for improvement on the method have been identified. The paper is the first review of the MPM and presents a state of the art of the current MPM literature covering 339 references.

The SPH fluid model (DualSPHysics) can deal with flow non-linearities, free-surface and intense topological changes, while the non-smooth dynamics model (Project Chrono) deals with discontinuous frictional contacts and kinematic restrictions. An open-source integrated framework to model fluid–structure–structure coupled systems is presented by implementing Project Chrono under DualSPHysics. The model is validated with fluid–structure–structure interaction cases. Both frictional and multi-restriction based behaviors are tested and simple convergence analysis are presented, showing that the model is capable of reproducing complex interactions. Several hypothetical cases are then presented, in order to demonstrate possible applications, showcasing a wide set of options useful for practitioners requiring the use of advanced fluid-mechanism models.

The structure model is set based on MPS-based discretization of linear and angular momenta corresponding to an isotropic elastic solid. Fluid-structure coupling is conducted in a mathematically-physically consistent manner along with implementation of a multi-resolution scheme comprising of common radius of influence, revised weight function, revised number density and potential number density concepts to enhance i) consistency of particle-based discretizations, ii) imposition of boundary conditions and iii) volume conservation at fluid-structure interface. The robustness and efficiency of proposed Enhanced Multi-resolution MPS-MPS FSI solver are investigated through a set of ocean engineering-related benchmark tests. To the best knowledge of authors, this study presents the first multi-resolution particle method for FSI corresponding to incompressible fluid and elastic structures.

10.1016/j.cma.2017.06.010.abstract: Abstract We seek to accelerate and increase the size of simulations for fluid–structure interactions (FSI) by using multiple resolutions in the spatial discretization of the equations governing the time evolution of systems displaying two-way fluid–solid coupling. To this end, we propose a multi-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) approach in which subdomains of different resolutions are directly coupled without any overlap region. The second-order consistent discretization of spatial differential operators is employed to ensure the accuracy of the proposed method. As SPH particles advect with the flow, a dynamic SPH particle refinement/coarsening is employed via splitting/merging to maintain a predefined multi-resolution configuration. Particle regularity is enforced via a particle-shifting technique to ensure accuracy and stability of the Lagrangian particle-based method embraced. The convergence, accuracy, and efficiency attributes of the new method are assessed by simulating four different flows. In this process, the numerical results are compared to the analytical, finite element, and consistent SPH single-resolution solutions. We anticipate that the proposed multi-resolution method will enlarge the class of SPH-tractable FSI applications.

10.1016/j.cma.2018.06.029.abstract: Abstract An efficient and accurate method is proposed to solve the incompressible flow momentum and continuity equations in computational domains partitioned into subdomains in the framework of the smoothed particle hydrodynamics method. The procedure does not require any overlap of the subdomains, which would result in the increase of the computational effort. Perfectly matching solutions are obtained at the surfaces separating neighboring blocks. The block interfaces can be both planar and curved surfaces allowing to easily decompose even geometrically complex domains. The smoothing length of the kernel function is maintained constant in each subdomain, while changing between blocks where a different resolution is required. Particles leaving each block through the interfaces are deactivated and correspondingly new particles are generated at the neighboring block using a dynamically adaptive procedure to control their frequency of release. No splitting and coalescing method is thus employed to take into account the different size and mass of the particles going through the interfaces. Mass conservation is guaranteed during the procedure, which is a challenging task in a Lagrangian method based on the domain decomposition. The test cases in both 2D and 3D approximation show the accuracy of the method and its ability to strongly reduce the computational efforts through a multi-resolution approach.

The method combines several attributes that have not been simultaneously satisfied by other SPH methods. Specifically, it employs the second-order consistent discretization for differential operators; it allows for resolutions spatially adapted with moving (translating and rotating) boundaries of arbitrary geometries; and, it accelerates the FSI solution as the adaptive approach leads to fewer degrees of freedom without sacrificing accuracy. The key ingredients in the method are a posteriori error estimator/distance-based criterion of adaptivity and a particle-shifting technique. The method is applied in simulating six different flows or FSI problems in two dimensions. The new method’s convergence, accuracy, and efficiency attributes are assessed by comparing the results it produces with analytical, finite element, and consistent SPH uniform high-resolution solutions as well as experimental data.

10.1016/j.cma.2022.114809.abstract: The inherent nonlinearity of free surface fluid–structure interaction (FSI) problems challenges numerical methods in terms of efficiency and fidelity. In this article, we propose an immersed finite element material point method for the water entry fluid–structure interaction problems. In this method, the fluid domain is discretized by an improved incompressible material point method (iMPM) using both Eulerian and Lagrangian descriptions, while the solid domain is solved by finite element method (FEM). The interaction between the iMPM and FEM is handled by a sharp immersed interface approach. Moreover, weighted tracing points are designed to track the fluid–structure interface with a low time complexity; a particle rearranging method is developed to eliminate the numerical cavities, which are non-physical voids caused by the highly disordered particle distribution, from which the original iMPM for FSI problems suffers. Various free surface FSI problems are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed method. The computational results are compared with analytical, experimental, and simulation data from the literature, with good agreement in cases where such data is available. The proposed method is expected to be a powerful tool for free surface FSI problems.

10.1016/j.cma.2022.115019.abstract: In this paper we propose an accurate, and computationally eﬃcient method for incorporating adaptive spatial resolution into weakly-compressible Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) schemes. Particles are adaptively split and merged in an accurate manner. Critically, the method ensures that the number of neighbors of each particle is optimal, leading to an eﬃcient algorithm. A set of background particles is used to specify either geometry-based spatial resolution, where the resolution is a function of distance to a solid body, or solution-based adaptive resolution, where the resolution is a function of the computed solution. This allows us to simulate problems using particles having length variations of the order of 1:250 with much fewer particles than currently reported with other techniques. The method is designed to automatically adapt when any solid bodies move. The algorithms employed are fully parallel. We consider a suite of benchmark problems to demonstrate the accuracy of the approach. We then consider the classic problem of the ﬂow past a circular cylinder at a range of Reynolds numbers and show that the proposed method produces accurate results with a signiﬁcantly reduced number of particles. We provide an open source implementation and a fully reproducible manuscript.

10.1016/j.cma.2022.115356.abstract: The multi-resolution method, e.g., the Adaptive Particle Reﬁnement (APR) method, has been developed to increase the local particle resolution and therefore the solution qual-ity within a pre-deﬁned reﬁnement zone instead of using a globally uniform resolution for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH). However, sometimes, the targeted zone of interest can be varying, and the corresponding topology is very complex, thus the conventional APR method is not able to track these characteristics adaptively. In this study, a novel Block-based Adaptive Particle Reﬁnement (BAPR) method is developed, which is able to provide the necessary local reﬁnement ﬂexibly for any targeted characteristic, and track it adaptively. In BAPR, the so-called activation status of the block array deﬁnes the reﬁnement regions, where the transition and activated zones are determined accordingly. A regularization method for the generated particles in the newly activated blocks is developed to render an isotropic distribution of these new particles. The proposed method has been deployed for simulating Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems. A set of 2D FSI cases have been simulated with the proposed BAPR method, and the performance of the BAPR method is quantiﬁed and validated comprehensively. In a word, the BAPR method is vi-able and potential for complex multi-resolution FSI simulations by tracking any targeted characteristic of interest.

10.1016/j.commatsci.2026.114839.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are changing the way researchers interact with code and data in scientific computing. While their ability to generate general-purpose code is well established, their effectiveness in producing scientifically valid scripts for domain-specific language (DSLs) remains largely unexplored. We propose an evaluation procedure that enables domain experts to assess the validity of LLM-generated input files for LAMMPS, a widely used molecular dynamics (MD) code, without requiring deep familiarity with its syntax. The evaluation procedure combines a normalization step that produces canonical input files with an extensible parser for syntax analysis, followed by a reduced-cost execution stage and accuracy checks that isolate common errors before running costly simulations. We apply the pipeline to eight state-of-the-art LLMs across three prompts of increasing complexity. The parser pass rate has improved from 74% to 91% over the past year, but scientific accuracy on coupled multi-step workflows remains limited. Across all 80 scripts evaluated on the most complex prompt, only one was fully correct as generated. We further package the automated stages as a reusable agentic skill that LLMs can invoke during script generation; in a small-scale demonstration, this skill helped two models produce five fully correct scripts out of six across the same three prompts, including the hardest one. The pipeline highlights both the limitations of current LLMs in generating scientific DSLs and a practical path toward integrating them into domain-specific computational ecosystems.
